title: Gray-Zone Warfare Picks Easy Targets in Germany
gist: Elisabeth Braw argues that gray-zone attackers (likely Russia, in Germany's case) target countries based on vulnerability rather than political stance — meaning decades of German diplomatic cooperativeness bought it no protection — and documents a specific drone-with-explosives incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport, an AfD-linked election disinformation campaign, and a foreign-intelligence surveillance operation against a German drone-maker CEO, concluding that public vigilance, not appeasement, is the only effective defense.

themes.theme: Vulnerability, not political stance, determines gray-zone targeting

insights.claim: Braw's core framework, developed over more than a decade of tracking gray-zone actions: aggressors don't target countries, sectors, or groups because they're high-profile or combative — they target them because they are low-hanging fruit, meaning a state's stance (hostile or cooperative) toward the aggressor matters far less than its vulnerability.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: A generalizable risk framework: any government or company assuming that diplomatic goodwill or non-confrontation reduces gray-zone attack risk is likely wrong — vulnerability assessment, not political posture, should drive defensive resource allocation.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Why would anyone want to harm'

insights.claim: Germany, despite decades of promoting peace and cooperation — co-founding the EU, participating in Iran nuclear deal negotiations, pursuing diplomatic talks over Russia's 2014 Ukraine attacks, and reunifying via orderly negotiation in 1990 — has still become a prime gray-zone target, proving that its earnest cooperative sentiments provided no protection.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Directly falsifies the theory that diplomatic appeasement reduces hybrid-warfare risk — a strategic lesson for any government (or company) considering conciliatory postures toward Russia or other gray-zone actors as a risk-mitigation strategy.
insights.quote: Political appeasement won't buy off hostile powers.

insights.claim: Germany today is as likely to be a gray-zone target as Estonia, which has for years loudly warned of Russian threats, even though Germany used to be highly moderate in its criticism of Russia — and it gets no credit for decades of cooperative effort despite now being as forceful in its Russia criticism as Estonia.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: A direct comparative data point (Germany = Estonia in targeting likelihood) that should recalibrate any country-risk model assuming hawkish, outspoken states face materially higher gray-zone attack risk than accommodating ones.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'That has led to the paradoxical reality'

insights.claim: A sophisticated drone equipped with anti-detection technology was found at Leipzig/Halle Airport — a crucial military-supply hub for Ukraine — after making a clumsy landing that caused it to accidentally drop its load of 600 grams of semtex, a high-grade explosive, on the ground nearby.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: A concrete, quantified incident (600 grams of semtex) at a military-logistics-critical airport for Ukraine is a hard data point for assessing the real physical-security risk facing European logistics infrastructure supporting Ukraine.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'What does this look like on the ground'

insights.claim: An almost-certainly Russia-sponsored online disinformation campaign flooded the internet ahead of September state elections in Saxony-Anhalt (where AfD polls above 40 percent) and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern (where AfD is the largest party at around 36 percent) with fake content discrediting other candidates, including personal targeting of Stefan Thumann, CEO of drone-supplier-to-Ukraine Donaustahl.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence of foreign election interference favoring a specific German party (AfD, which is more sympathetic to Russia) ahead of September state elections — a trackable, dated event with direct implications for German political risk and defense-sector supply-chain security (via the Donaustahl targeting).
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'An online campaign, almost certainly sponsored by Russia'

insights.claim: German authorities arrested a Ukrainian man and a Romanian woman this month who had been tracking Donaustahl CEO Stefan Thumann's daily life, including visiting his home, after a tip from a foreign ally; German prosecutors accused them of acting on behalf of a foreign intelligence agency.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Physical surveillance/targeting of a mid-sized defense-supply-chain executive (drone supplier to Ukraine) confirms gray-zone threats now extend to personal physical security of European defense-industrial executives, not just infrastructure — relevant for corporate security planning at defense-linked firms.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Because Donaustahl is not a high-profile company'

insights.claim: Russian hackers stole images from CCTV and door cameras across Europe earlier this year and published them to mock Western authorities, and Russian transmitters have for many months been jamming and spoofing GPS signals in the Baltic Sea region, making navigation much harder for ships and aircraft.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Ongoing GPS jamming/spoofing in the Baltic Sea is a persistent, unresolved navigational-safety hazard for European maritime and aviation traffic — a live operational risk factor for Baltic shipping insurance and logistics planning.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Earlier this year, Russian hackers'

insights.claim: Iran is not just a regional actor: cyber teams thought to be linked to Iran attacked water treatment plants in small Minnesota towns this summer, targeting relatively easy targets in a blue state locked in a battle with the Trump administration, apparently caring less about political positions than opportunistic vulnerability.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Confirms gray-zone tactics against U.S. domestic infrastructure (not just European targets) attributed to Iran, reinforcing that critical-infrastructure vulnerability, not political alignment, is the deciding factor for targeting — relevant for U.S. municipal water-infrastructure cybersecurity risk assessment.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Russia is not the world's only perpetrator'

themes.theme: Asymmetric cost-benefit favors attackers; vigilance is the only defense

insights.claim: Because Western countries don't retaliate eye-for-eye or at all, gray-zone perpetrators can keep testing targets with an extremely advantageous cost-benefit calculus — some attacks succeed, some fail, but failure carries no real cost, a dynamic Braw calls 'the defender's dilemma' in her book of the same name.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Names and frames a structural asymmetry ('the defender's dilemma') that should inform how governments and firms budget for gray-zone defense — since attackers face near-zero downside, expect a persistently high and rising volume of probing attacks across sectors.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'In fact, perpetrators of gray-zone activities'

insights.claim: At Leipzig/Halle Airport, it was an eagle-eyed airport worker who first spotted the drone in the middle of the night — Braw's conclusion is that keeping the public informed and alert, not maintaining a low political profile, is the more effective defense against gray-zone threats.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: A concrete, actionable policy recommendation (public vigilance over diplomatic appeasement) for governments designing gray-zone defense strategy — relevant for security-sector policy and infrastructure-worker training investment.
insights.quote: Being nice is good. Staying alert is better.
